Eighth Commandment
AYTH kuh-MAND-muhnt
noun (the Decalogue)
From the eighth word of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:15; commandment from Latin mandare, to charge.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Eighth Commandment is the word of the Decalogue that guards property and honest dealing: "Thou shalt not steal" (Exod 20:15). It forbids the taking of what is another's by theft, robbery, fraud, false weights, oppression, the withholding of wages, usury, and every dishonest gain. By guarding the neighbor's goods it upholds the lawful right of property, which Scripture everywhere assumes — for one cannot steal what is held in common, and the command itself supposes that men rightly own what is theirs. Positively, it requires honest labor, fair dealing, the paying of debts and wages, faithful stewardship, and a generous hand to the poor: "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). So the commandment turns the thief into a worker and the worker into a giver. It reaches the heart, forbidding covetousness, the root of theft, and the greed that is idolatry (Col 3:5). This dictionary confesses the Eighth Commandment as binding moral law, upholding both the right of property and the duty of charity, and condemning theft whether done by the burglar, the swindler, the oppressor of the poor, or the tax-gatherer who robs by the color of law.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The word of the Decalogue guarding property and honest dealing (Exod 20:15): "Thou shalt not steal." It forbids theft, fraud, false weights, oppression, and dishonest gain; upholds the lawful right of property; and requires honest labor, fair dealing, and a generous hand to the needy (Eph 4:28).

EIGHTH COMMANDMENT, noun. The eighth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:15), guarding property and honest dealing.

"Thou shalt not steal" — forbidding theft, robbery, fraud, false weights, and oppression.

Upholds the lawful right of property, which the command itself assumes.

Requires honest labor, fair dealing, the paying of wages, and faithful stewardship.

Turns the thief into a worker and the worker into a giver (Eph 4:28).

📖 Key Scripture

Exod 20:15 — "Thou shalt not steal."

Eph 4:28 — "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth."

Lev 19:13 — "Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning."

Prov 11:1 — "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Eighth Commandment is corrupted by those who keep its letter while breaking its spirit — the respectable fraud, the unjust weight, the withheld wage — and by ideologies that deny the right of property the commandment upholds, calling the redistribution of another man's goods justice rather than the theft it is.

expand to see more

The first corruption is the gentleman thief: the man who would never break into a house but defrauds in his business, uses a false balance (Prov 11:1), withholds the laborer's wage (Lev 19:13), or profits by oppressing the poor. The commandment reaches all of these. Theft wears a suit as often as a mask, and the dictionary names the respectable forms — fraud, exploitation, the dishonest gain dressed as good business — as true breaches of the Eighth Commandment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but a deeper corruption denies the very right of property the commandment assumes. Ideologies that treat private ownership as itself oppression, and the seizing of another man's goods as justice, stand the commandment on its head: "thou shalt not steal" presupposes that a man may rightly own. The principle to recover is the whole counsel: the right of property is real and guarded, and so is the duty of charity — honest labor that one may have to give to him that needeth (Eph 4:28). The commandment condemns both the burglar and the system that robs by law, and commands the open hand.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the eighth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:15); the commandment forbidding theft and fraud, upholding the right of property and the duty of honest labor and charity.

Exodus 20:15 — the eighth word of the Decalogue

"Thou shalt not steal" — Hebrew ganav, to steal, carry off

Usage

"The Eighth Commandment condemns the swindler and the false weight as surely as the burglar."

""Thou shalt not steal" assumes the right of property the Eighth Commandment guards."

"The Eighth Commandment turns the thief into a worker who labors that he may give."
